nameStory: The name 'lobed coreopsis' comes from its distinctively lobed leaves that set it apart from other tickseeds. The alternate common name 'mouse-ear tickseed' refers to how the rounded, fuzzy leaf lobes resemble tiny mouse ears. All coreopsis species are called 'tickseed' because their small, dark seeds reminded early botanists of ticks clinging to fur.
description: Lobed coreopsis is a cheerful perennial wildflower with bright yellow, daisy-like blooms and distinctively shaped leaves. It grows as a low-growing clump about 1-2 feet tall and wide, spreading by underground stems to form colonies. The plant produces sunny golden flowers on slender stems above a mound of unusual lobed foliage. Though native to the southeastern United States, it occasionally appears in New England gardens and naturalized areas.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The leaves are the key identifying feature - they're deeply lobed with rounded segments that feel soft and slightly fuzzy, resembling mouse ears or mittens with fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with 8 broad, notched petals surrounding a darker yellow center, blooming from late spring through summer on thin, wiry stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading clumps that hug the ground, rarely exceeding 2 feet in height but can spread several feet wide through creeping roots

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Flower stems are slender, smooth, and rise well above the foliage mound, swaying gently in breezes and feeling wiry to the touch

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark, flattened seeds with tiny wing-like edges that cling to clothing and pet fur, explaining the 'tickseed' nickname

habitat: In New England, lobed coreopsis is extremely rare and found mainly in cultivated gardens or areas where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers well-drained soils in sunny to partially shaded locations. When naturalized, it typically appears in disturbed areas, field edges, or abandoned garden sites where it can spread freely.

seasonality.spring: New fuzzy, lobed leaves emerge in early spring, forming distinctive rounded clumps. First flower buds begin to appear on elongating stems by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright yellow flowers opening continuously from June through August. Seeds begin forming on spent flower heads by mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall though less prolifically. Seeds ripen and disperse, while foliage may begin to yellow and die back with first frosts.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, leaving only dormant underground roots and stems to overwinter until spring regrowth.

funFact: Despite being called 'tickseed,' the seeds were actually used by Native Americans as a coffee substitute when roasted, and the flowers produce a beautiful yellow dye that was prized for coloring baskets and textiles.
confusionNotes: The deeply lobed, mouse-ear shaped leaves make this species nearly unmistakable among the coreopsis family. Other tickseeds have either narrow, lance-shaped leaves or simple oval leaves, but none have the distinctive rounded lobes of this species.
contextualKnowledge: Lobed coreopsis is sometimes called 'mouse-ear coreopsis' in garden centers, which can be confusing since there's also a completely different plant called 'mouse-ear chickweed.' Always check the scientific name Coreopsis auriculata when purchasing to ensure you're getting the right plant.
compareHints: Among New England's coreopsis species, lobed coreopsis is immediately distinguished by its uniquely shaped leaves - rose coreopsis has narrow linear leaves, lance-leaved has simple spear-shaped leaves, and whorled coreopsis has thread-like leaves in circles around the stem. The soft, fuzzy, deeply-lobed foliage of lobed coreopsis looks completely different from any of its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rose Coreopsis is the only tickseed in New England with pink or white petals - all its relatives like Lance-leaved and Whorled Coreopsis have bright yellow flowers.
Among its tickseed relatives, Whorled Coreopsis is the only one with thread-like leaves arranged in distinct whorls around the stem.

Lance-leaved Coreopsis differs from other Coreopsis species by its simple, unlobed lance-shaped leaves - Rose Coreopsis has much smaller pink flowers, while Whorled Coreopsis has very finely divided, thread-like leaves.
Plains coreopsis differs from other New England coreopsis species by being an annual (dies each year) rather than perennial, and by having the most deeply divided, feathery leaves of the group.
Tall coreopsis dwarfs all other New England coreopsis species - most relatives like lance-leaved coreopsis and rose coreopsis stay under 3 feet tall.

Large-flowered tickseed stands out from other New England tickseeds by its size - both the flowers and overall plant are notably larger than rose coreopsis (which has pink flowers) or lance-leaved coreopsis.

Unlike its New England relatives like Lance-leaved Coreopsis (which has simple, narrow leaves) or Rose Coreopsis (which has thin, needle-like leaves), Prairie Coreopsis has those distinctive deeply-divided, finger-like leaves that make it unmistakable.
